name: Patchouli

lead: Patchouli is the essential oil of a tropical mint-family plant, Pogostemon cablin, and one of perfumery's best-known base notes. Its scent is heavy, earthy, woody and balsamic, and it appears in many masculine, unisex and oriental fragrances.

For looks and presentation it works as part of grooming: a fragrance with patchouli in the base tends to linger on skin and clothing. Lab and animal studies have looked at the plant's compounds for other effects, but those are not scent studies.

paras: People encounter it as a note in colognes and perfumes, in scented soaps and grooming products, and as a pure essential oil or incense. In fragrance communities it is described as a base note and is often blended with other woods and resins.

A toxicologic review of patchouli alcohol as a fragrance ingredient exists [4]. Like other essential oils it can irritate or sensitise skin in some people, and concentrated oil is usually diluted in products. The 1960s hippie association colours how some people perceive the smell.

chain: Patchouli oil is blended into a fragrance base
The base note lingers on skin and clothing
A distinctive, warm scent adds to personal presentation
angle.text: Patchouli gives colognes an earthy, long-lasting base. People who wear it use scent as part of grooming, the way they use a haircut or clothing.

lead: Patchouli is a fragrant material obtained by steam distillation of the dried leaves and twigs of Pogostemon cablin, a bushy perennial in the mint family native to the island region of Southeast Asia.[1] Its scent is described as heavy, strong, woody, earthy, balsamic and spicy, and the main component of the oil is patchoulol, a sesquiterpene alcohol.[1]

In grooming it matters because scent is part of how a person comes across. Perfumers use patchouli as a base note in masculine and unisex fragrances and in scented personal products such as bay rum.[1] Because the oil evaporates slowly and gives a composition body, perfumers use it to make a fragrance last on skin and clothing; fragrance writers describe it as the foundation under lighter notes.[2] The oil is also found in incense, repellents and household products.[1]

Its reputation has swung between luxury and counterculture: dried leaves packed with imported shawls made it fashionable in 19th-century Europe, and the 1960s and 1970s hippie movement made it a signature scent, after which it became a quieter ingredient before niche perfumers began featuring it again.[1][2] Beyond perfumery, researchers have studied patchouli constituents in the lab and in animals, including photoprotection in mouse skin and stress responses in a small human trial.[3][4] Verbal context has also been shown to change how people rate its smell.[5]

paras: The plant grows up to about 75 cm tall with erect stems and small pale pink-white flowers, and it does best in warm, humid tropical climates.[1] It is native to Southeast Asian islands, including the Malay Peninsula, Indonesia and the Philippines, and also occurs in parts of Nepal and northeast India.[1] Seed-producing flowers are rare, so growers usually propagate it from cuttings rooted in loamy soil.[1] The name comes from the Tamil word paccuḷi.[1]

The essential oil is made by steam distillation of dried leaves and twigs. Cell walls must first be ruptured, by steam scalding, light fermentation or drying, and the plant can be harvested several times a year. Wikipedia notes that sources disagree on the best method, some favouring distillation of fresh or partly dried leaf near the harvest site and others favouring boiling and fermenting dried leaves.[1]

Patchoulol is the main constituent, and commercial oils are often graded by their patchoulol content. Other components include germacrene B, norpatchoulenol and pogostone.[1] Grokipedia gives a yield of about 2.6% of leaf weight and puts patchoulol at up to 72% of the oil, with α-guaiene and α-bulnesene also present.[6] Global demand was above 1,600 metric tons a year as of 2023, with more than 90% produced in Indonesia; the most common commercial varieties come from Sumatra and Sulawesi.[1]

Wikipedia says patchouli has been used in perfume for centuries and is an important ingredient in East Asian incense.[1] Grokipedia adds that traditional Chinese and Ayurvedic medicine used the herb, and that 19th-century European trade used leaves from Asia to scent fabrics and shawls, building its image as an exotic luxury.[6] According to a perfume house's history essay, dried leaves were packed with Indian cashmere shawls to repel moths, so the scent became linked with authentic Indian goods and European makers began scenting their own shawls; the oil was fashionable by mid-century.[2]

As patchouli became cheap and widely sold it lost its luxury image, and in the 1960s and 1970s the counterculture adopted it as a signature scent.[2] Wikipedia reports that patchouli oil and incense surged in popularity in the United States and Europe in those decades, largely through the hippie movement.[1] The same essay says the association left the material seeming unfashionable by the 1980s, when marketers often left it unnamed even though perfumers kept using it for body and longevity in woody and base accords. It describes niche houses beginning to feature patchouli openly from the late 1990s, often using aged, heart-cut oil, and a cleaner, woody captive molecule introduced around 2014.[2] Grokipedia credits aged oil with giving depth to oriental and chypre compositions.[6]

Modern uses include perfumery, scented personal products such as bay rum, incense, and industrial products such as paper towels, detergents and air fresheners.[1] In perfumery it is classed as a base note. Fragrance writers say its slow evaporation lends longevity and body to other notes and helps a scent stay on skin and clothing, which is why a patchouli base appears in many masculine, unisex and oriental fragrances.[1][2]

Wikipedia also records other uses: leaves are used in herbal tea, as a vegetable or seasoning in some cultures, and in traditional Chinese medicine for colds, nausea, diarrhea, headache and fever. In 1985 Mattel used patchouli oil in the plastic of the Stinkor action figure.[1]

Laboratory and animal work has examined patchouli constituents for non-fragrance effects. Pogostone, a constituent of the oil, reduced markers of UV skin damage in mice, which the authors attributed to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action.[3] Other animal and review papers have examined patchouli alcohol or the oil in models of depression-like behaviour, obesity, colitis, irritable bowel syndrome and smoke-induced lung inflammation, and a review of volatile oils from herbal medicines covers the wider area.[7][8][9][10][11][12] A 38-oil screen on volunteers' forearms found undiluted patchouli among the oils that gave longer protection from mosquito bites than most.[13]

A fragrance material review addresses the toxicology and dermatology of patchouli alcohol as a perfume ingredient.[14] Wikipedia also notes that patchouli is a potent repellent against the Formosan subterranean termite and that pogostone has been tested for antimicrobial activity.[1]

Human research is limited. A randomized controlled trial in emergency nurses studied short-term patchouli oil inhalation and its effect on professional quality of life and stress levels.[4] A study of 38 essential oils on volunteers' forearms assessed mosquito repellency.[13] A randomized study found that verbal labels changed how people perceived odors including patchouli.[5] No trials were found on patchouli and attractiveness or appearance.

lore.intro: Patchouli is discussed mostly by perfumers and fragrance writers, who describe it as a base-note material and as a scent with strong cultural associations.[1][2]
